Monday, Tanuja had a half-built cardboard model of her water-testing kit and an urge to hide it until it looked neat. Her mentor, Naveen sir, was free at four. She almost skipped it.
Tuesday, red-faced, she put the rough model on his desk. He turned it over and said, "Your sensor sits above the waterline. It will never touch the sample." She felt small and relieved at once.
Friday, she rebuilt the base with the sensor lower. It took an afternoon. She thought about the three weeks she would have spent building on the wrong plan.

qa.q: When did Tanuja put the rough model on the mentor's desk?
qa.a: She put the rough cardboard model on Naveen sir's desk on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she put the model on the desk?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed because the model was rough, but also relieved that the mistake was found early.

qa.q: What did Tanuja change after the feedback?
qa.a: She rebuilt the base with the sensor set lower, which took only an afternoon.

qa.q: How does Naveen sir see the rough model?
qa.a: Naveen sir treats it as something he can check quickly and correct at once, so an early look saves Tanuja from a long wrong build.

grounding: Shows a student sharing a rough model with a mentor early despite embarrassment and avoiding weeks of building the wrong thing.

passage: I am Swati, and I want to tell you about my thesis year. I had planned three weeks to build a survey on how buses run late in my town. I was ashamed of my outline, one messy page, so I nearly waited till it was perfect. My guide, Sabina ma'am, had a free hour, so I took the page to her, blushing. She read it and said, "A report from two years ago already has this answer. Use their numbers, and ask what they missed." I sat in the corridor afterwards, half stunned. Three weeks saved. That mess of a page was the cheapest thing I ever showed anyone.

qa.q: How long had Swati planned to spend building the survey?
qa.a: Swati had planned three weeks to build the survey.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling as Swati took the outline to Sabina ma'am?
qa.a: Swati was blushing and ashamed of the messy page, but went anyway.

qa.q: What choice by Swati saved weeks of work?
qa.a: Taking the messy outline to Sabina ma'am early, instead of waiting until it was perfect.

qa.q: What did Sabina ma'am see in the outline that Swati had missed?
qa.a: Sabina ma'am knew a report from two years ago already had the answer, so she could point Swati to use those numbers and look for what was missing.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling showing a rough outline to a mentor early despite embarrassment and saving weeks of wasted building.

passage: Pankaj, twenty, was designing a low-cost water filter for his diploma project at the polytechnic in a small town near Kolhapur. After three days of sketches, he had a rough drawing full of crossings-out. He wanted to wait until it looked professional before showing his mentor, Ramesh sir. But the deadline for materials was close. Embarrassed, he took the messy sheet to the workshop. Ramesh sir looked at it for a minute. "The sand layer is fine. But this clay pipe will crack when you heat it. Use a steel one." Pankaj's ears burned. Then he realised: if he'd built it first, he'd have lost two weeks and all his material money. He redrew the pipe that evening.

qa.q: What did Ramesh sir say would crack?
qa.a: The clay pipe would crack when heated.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel taking the messy sheet to his mentor?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his ears burning, because the drawing wasn't polished.

qa.q: Why was showing the rough drawing early a good choice?
qa.a: It revealed the pipe problem before building, saving two weeks and his material money.

qa.q: How might Ramesh sir see the rough drawing?
qa.a: Ramesh sir likely saw it as useful rather than messy, since early drafts are the easiest to correct.

grounding: Shows a student showing a rough, messy draft to his mentor despite embarrassment and avoiding a costly wrong build.

passage: Selin, twenty-one, was writing her first research essay in history at a university in Izmir. After a week she had two scruffy pages and an outline full of question marks. Her tutor Esther held drop-in hours on Tuesdays. Selin nearly didn't go; showing something so rough felt like showing up in pyjamas. She went anyway, clutching the pages. Esther read for five minutes. "Your question is interesting. But these three sources are about a different century." Selin's face went hot. Esther smiled. "Better now than after you've written ten pages." Selin walked out with the right sources, feeling exposed but lighter. She would have spent two weeks on the wrong period.

qa.q: On which day did Esther hold drop-in hours?
qa.a: On Tuesdays.

qa.q: How did Selin feel about taking her rough pages to Esther?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and exposed, as if showing up in pyjamas.

qa.q: What did Selin gain by showing the draft early?
qa.a: She found out that her sources were about a different century, saving two weeks of work in the wrong direction.

qa.q: How does Esther see early rough drafts?
qa.a: Esther sees them as the best time for feedback, saying it is better now than after ten pages.

grounding: Shows a student bringing a rough draft to a tutor early despite embarrassment and saving days of work in the wrong direction.

passage: In the university's design lab, Bidisha, nineteen, had to build an app prototype for a campus food-ordering service. After two evenings, she had rough paper sketches of four screens, drawn in pencil. Her mentor, Samir, a final-year student, passed her desk. She almost flipped the sheets over. Instead she said, "They're really rough, but can you look?" He studied them. "The menu is great. But nobody will find the pay button hidden at the bottom." She winced. "Also, canteen staff need a screen too." She hadn't thought of that at all. That night she redrew the screens. A week later, her classmates who had coded full apps first were rebuilding theirs.

qa.q: How many screens had Bidisha sketched?
qa.a: Four screens.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when Samir passed her desk?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and exposed, almost flipping the rough sheets over.

qa.q: Why did asking for feedback on paper sketches pay off?
qa.a: It revealed the hidden pay button and the missing staff screen before any coding, when fixes were cheap.

qa.q: How might Bidisha's classmates feel a week later?
qa.a: They are likely frustrated, having to rebuild the full apps they coded before asking for feedback.

grounding: Shows a student showing rough paper sketches early despite embarrassment, avoiding days of building in the wrong direction.

passage:
Subject: Thank you for looking at the messy draft
Dear Dr Jaya,
I nearly didn't send you those interview questions last Monday. They were half in Hindi, half in English, with notes like "??? ask better" in the margins, and I was embarrassed that you'd think I hadn't worked at all. I sent them at 11:58 pm so I couldn't change my mind.
I'm glad I did. Your comment that my questions asked vendors to judge the municipality, instead of describing their day, saved me. I had planned to print 60 copies and start interviews at the Sadar market on Saturday. I would have spent two weeks collecting answers to the wrong question.
I've rewritten them to begin with "Tell me about yesterday, from when you opened your stall." Attached. Still rough, but rough in the right direction this time.
Thank you,
Darshan

qa.q: How many copies had Darshan planned to print?
qa.a: 60 copies.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling before sending the draft?
qa.a: Darshan was embarrassed about how rough the questions looked and nervous enough to send them at 11:58 pm to avoid backing out.

qa.q: What did sending the rough draft early save Darshan from?
qa.a: It saved two weeks of interviews at the Sadar market built on the wrong question, fixed before any copies were printed.

qa.q: How might Dr Jaya feel getting a messy draft early rather than a polished one late?
qa.a: Dr Jaya probably finds it easy and satisfying to help at that stage, when one comment can turn the project before real effort is wasted.

grounding: Shows a student who shares a rough draft with a mentor early despite embarrassment and avoids days of work in the wrong direction.
